# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# A Close Reading of the Varga & Holm Comment

**The comment's claim.** Using the Halden microdata, the authors show that attrition, a manager-reported output measure, and a scheduled-hours denominator inflated the headline gain. Correcting the last two cuts the gain from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset where correction is possible. They then argue that the remaining gain is novelty, and conclude that per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact".

The first half of the comment is strong and important. The second half overreaches in the opposite direction from Halden. The data support "the gain is about half what was reported, and its durability is untested". They do not support "the gain is entirely an artifact."

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition (§1).** This is the most serious finding. The working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata show seven of nine withdrew *after the schedule began*, and six of nine cited workload or output. That goes beyond a limitation: the working paper misdescribed its own data. Halden's authors should be asked to respond.
- **Output measure (§2).** Managers rated output above the records in 19 of 23 organisations. That is a clear, systematic bias, and the comment is fair in not alleging bad faith.
- **Hours (§3).** Time-tracking data show hours fell about 14%, not 20%. This is consistent with Varden, where timesheets showed 13% in backlog work.
- **Revenue (§4).** Deflating 1.4% nominal growth by 4.1% inflation gives roughly −2.6% real, which is correct.
- **Sectors (§5).** The point that per-hour metrics turn any output above 80 into a "gain" is right, and the record-based retail figure of −11.2% strengthens it.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures check out:

- Table 1 difference: 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8.
- Table 2: 95.1 / 0.8 → +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 → +14.6%; 95.4 / 0.861 → +10.8%.
- Hours ratios: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859; 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861.
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ 0.974.

**One inconsistency.** The hours decomposition in §3 doesn't add up. Four scheduled days of 8 hours plus 0.7 hours a day is 34.8, and adding 1.6 hours on the day off gives **about 36.4 hours**, not 34.6. Starting from the 40.3-hour baseline makes it worse, at about 36.6. For the 34.6 figure to hold, the longer days must add only about 0.25 hours each, or the day-off figure is wrong.

If 36.4 is the correct total, hours fell only about 10%, and the corrected per-hour gain would be **smaller** than 10.8%. Either way the authors need to reconcile these numbers.

## Where it overreaches

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the data note

The data note says, correctly, that the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole". The abstract and conclusion then go much further: per-hour gains "reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general are "entirely an artifact". That leaps from a 17-organisation subset of one pilot to every scheme.

The abstract also says four problems "account for most of the reported gain", then claims the gain is entirely artifact. These are different claims, and only the first is shown.

### 2. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

The only evidence offered is self-reported energy, measured at two time points and extrapolated in a straight line.

- **The extrapolation itself.** Energy fell 0.32 SD over three months, which gives zero around month 8.7, not ten. A straight line through two points can't tell a decline to baseline apart from a plateau.
- **Energy is not output.** A fall in reported energy does not show that output per hour fell.
- **A direct test was available and not run.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, record-based output per actual hour should decline over months 1–6. That trend is the obvious test, and leaving it out is the comment's largest gap.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming a durable effect" is fair against Halden. But "entirely an artifact" is itself a positive claim, and the same burden applies to it.

### 3. Varden is cited selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature" but does not mention the case-processing stratum of the same trial. That stratum uses the same design, administrative output and timesheet hours, and it found **+12.5% per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months**, three months past where Halden stopped. The comment omits this and does not explain why.

That estimate is very close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%. It comes from a randomised design with a control group, which also knew a trial was under way. That doesn't rule out novelty, but it is the best available evidence that a gain of this size survives proper measurement for at least nine months in backlog-type work.

The comment also leaves out that Varden's counter stratum showed **+6.7%** per actual hour. "Reduced hours reduce output where output depends on presence" is correct *per employee*. It is not the whole picture per hour, a distinction Varden draws explicitly.

### 4. Varden's meetings analysis is mischaracterised

- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known."** The seven offices are *all* the treated case-processing offices, not a selected subgroup. The data were collected at managers' request in month six. Varden reported this analysis as unregistered, rests on seven offices, cannot establish a mechanism, and has registered a confirmatory test. The comment repeats Varden's caveats back as criticisms.
- **Tension with the novelty argument.** Cancelled standing meetings are a structural change and need not fade like enthusiasm. If meetings account for much of the gain, which a back-of-envelope calculation from Varden's figures suggests, that is a *competing* explanation to novelty. It is not one to dismiss in support of it.
- **Halden's own interviews.** 47 of 58 Halden managers named meeting cuts unprompted. That's weak evidence, but it is consistent across both studies.

The right position is "an untested hypothesis with a registered test", not "should not be cited".

### 5. The record-based index has its own bias

Among the record types used, "billable hours delivered" is mechanically tied to hours worked. Where it served as the output measure, which is likely for professional services, the largest sector, a cut in hours lowers measured output by construction. The record-based index may therefore *understate* output for those organisations. The comment should report Table 1 by record type.

### 6. Attrition is better bounded than assumed

The attrition point is strong, but the comment only asserts that the nine were "plausibly the least successful". The recommended approach, analysing all enrolled organisations, could be partly applied now. A bounds analysis would turn §1 from a direction into a magnitude, for example:

- including the nine with any output data they have, or
- assigning them a range of assumed outcomes, from an index of 80 up to the survivors' mean.

## Smaller points

- **Revenue is not part of the per-hour correction.** It is listed among the "four problems" but plays no role in the per-hour figure, and the abstract correctly says "correcting the first three". The conclusion's tally is consistent; the framing in the abstract less so.
- **Deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue. Sector output-price deflators would be better, but the direction of the correction is surely right.
- **Not addressed.** The comment does not cover Halden's uncorrected seasonality for sick days and output, or the mechanical fall in sick days from fewer scheduled days. Both would strengthen its case.

## What the evidence supports

Across the three papers, a defensible reading is:

1. Halden's 23.4% is substantially inflated. Corrected for record-based output and actual hours in the subset with data, the gain is about 11%, possibly less once the hours inconsistency is resolved. This applies to organisations that did not withdraw, so it is an upper-leaning estimate.
2. Varden's randomised trial finds a gain of similar size (+12.5%) in backlog work at nine months, which argues against "entirely an artifact".
3. Where output depends on presence, output per employee falls and service gets worse. Both studies agree on this.
4. Whether the gain lasts, and whether it comes from rest, cut meetings or novelty, is open. Halden's monthly data and Varden's 24-month follow-up can address it.

## The pattern

Halden overstated a provisional result. This comment correctly takes the overstatement apart, then overstates the opposite conclusion: it attributes the residual to novelty without the test its own data allow, and cites only the half of Varden that supports it. It follows the "failures come in pairs" idea from the first document you shared, and the two errors here are the same mistake in opposite directions. The comment's §1–§4 should stand; §6–§8 should be cut back to what was shown.

I can draft a reply letter to the comment, a referee report, or a one-page synthesis of all three papers if useful.
